opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most important questions as these systems get more capable. In the near term, I imagine programmers will shift from writing every line themselves to being more like architects or editors. You specify what you want, the system proposes something, and your job becomes judging whether it's correct, elegant, and safe. That's already a different skill from writing code from scratch, and in some ways a harder one, because reading and verifying someone else's code is notoriously difficult.

As the systems get more powerful, I don't think we can rely only on humans eyeballing the output. The code will be too voluminous and possibly too clever for that. So we'll need to lean much more on tools. Rigorous testing, formal verification where it's feasible, and AI systems that help explain and audit what other AI systems have produced. You could imagine a system that writes the code and another that tries to break it, find edge cases, or prove properties about it. Then the human sits at the top of that stack, making sure the goals and specifications are right.

To me that's the crux. Correctly specifying what you actually want is going to become the most valuable skill. Many bugs, even today, come from people not fully understanding the problem rather than from typos in the implementation. If the AI handles more of the implementation, the human contribution moves upstream, to taste, judgment, and clarity of intent.

There's also a scientific angle that I care about a lot, which is interpretability. We want to understand not just whether the output works, but why the system produced it, so we can trust it in high-stakes settings. So I see it as a combination: better verification tools, AI helping to check AI, and humans focusing on the specification and the values behind it. And I think great programmers will still be enormously valuable, maybe more so, because they'll be able to do the work of whole teams if they use these tools well.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a separate AI system to audit code from the system that wrote it, including trying to break it and find edge cases.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a really interesting question, and it's one we think about a lot actually, because we're already seeing it internally. The first thing I'd say is that the relationship is going to change from one where you're reading and checking every line to one that's much more about specification and verification. So the human's job shifts up a level of abstraction. You become more like an architect, or almost like a scientist running experiments on the system, rather than someone inspecting the bricks.

And the key insight, I think, is that verification is often much easier than generation. This is true in mathematics, it's true in a lot of science, and it's true in programming. It's much easier to check that a proof is correct than to come up with it in the first place. So even if the system is producing code that's more sophisticated than what a given engineer would write themselves, you can still design tests, you can still specify what the behaviour should be, you can still look at the outputs and the properties of the code. That asymmetry is what makes the whole thing tractable.

Then the second thing is that you'll increasingly use AI systems to check other AI systems. So you'd have one model writing the code, another model acting as a critic, trying to find bugs, trying to find security holes, perhaps a third one trying to formally verify properties of it. And the human sits on top of that whole process, looking at where the systems disagree, because the disagreements are usually where the interesting things are. That's actually very similar to how we approached things like AlphaGo or AlphaFold, where you have a generator and some form of evaluation working against each other.

Now, I don't want to be naive about it. There is a real risk that as the systems get more capable, humans become sort of complacent, you just trust the output because it's been right the last hundred times. And that's exactly the moment it becomes dangerous. So I think there's going to need to be a lot of work on interpretability, on having systems explain their reasoning in a way that's actually faithful to what they did, not just a plausible story after the fact. We're putting a lot of effort into that at DeepMind, because for the really high-stakes domains, in medicine, in critical infrastructure, you can't just say "the tests passed." You need to understand why it works.

And I'd say the last point is that programmers will need to understand the systems themselves, almost as a new kind of literacy. Not just the code that's produced, but the strengths and the failure modes of the thing producing it. Where does it tend to hallucinate an API that doesn't exist? Where does it take shortcuts? That becomes part of the craft. So I actually think it's quite an exciting time to be an engineer, as long as we build the right tools and keep the human genuinely in the loop, rather than just nominally in the loop.

r001.rationale: It proposes using a separate AI model as a critic and another to formally verify code produced by the code-generating model.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll move toward a situation where the programmer is specifying what they want the system to do, and then assessing whether it’s actually achieved that, rather than necessarily inspecting every line of code. But that raises a difficult question: if the system produces something very complex, how do you know it’s correct?

You’d want several layers of verification. You can test its behavior, you can ask it to explain its approach, and, where possible, you can use formal methods to prove particular properties. You might also have other AI systems trying to find flaws in what it’s written. An explanation alone isn’t enough—it could sound convincing and still be wrong.

So human programmers would still need a deep understanding of the problem. Their role might become more about asking the right questions, defining the constraints, and deciding what evidence would actually justify trusting the result. And I think that becomes especially important when the software is doing something consequential in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response proposes using “other AI systems” to find flaws in the generated code, distinct from the system that wrote it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the role of the programmer will shift toward specifying what they want the system to do, and then checking whether it actually does that. And those are both quite difficult problems. Often, when you start writing software, you discover that you hadn’t fully understood the problem you were trying to solve.

You don’t necessarily have to follow every step of how a solution was produced to assess it. You can run the code, test it, examine its behavior. But passing a set of tests isn’t the same as being correct, particularly if we’re talking about something critical, like medical software or infrastructure. There, I think we’ll want stronger guarantees, perhaps using formal verification where that’s possible.

We’ll also use AI systems to help scrutinize other AI systems’ code. But you have to be careful that they’re not all making the same mistake. The human still needs enough understanding to ask the right questions, challenge the assumptions, and decide what evidence would actually be convincing. So I think programming knowledge remains very valuable, even if people spend much less time writing individual lines of code.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems can help scrutinize other AI systems’ code, communicating use of a separate AI reviewer to assess generated code.
